title: Treasury Markets not as “Safe” as You Think - Systematic Investor - Ep.414

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Treasury Markets not as “Safe” as You Think - Systematic Investor - Ep.414.docx

speakers: Mark Rzepczynski (co-host, systematic/VUCA-focused quant, caption 'Mark Ramsinski')
summary: Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor, Aug 2026: Mark and Niels discuss market 'rumblings' (leverage blowups, Korean bubble, yen intervention, stock issuance), commodity buffer stocks, and the Treasury buyback and market plumbing (primary dealer capacity, hedge fund basis trade, repo leverage, March 2020). Also trend-following style taxonomy (LGT paper), blending styles as pods, tick size and short-term trend, and a tribute to Victor Niederhoffer.

coverage.note: intro; 'rumblings' list: leverage blowup, Korean stock bubble, issuance, yen intervention
concentrated bets at market makers; 177% single stock move and risk; stock vs futures volatility
market maker correlation risk; copper spread squeeze and commodity buffer stocks
oil inventories, China stock draw, blowoff risk; trend barometer; VUCA volatility view
complexity and ambiguity create trends; performance figures; Treasury action at long end
Treasury auction size, on-the-run vs off-the-run liquidity, buyback programme
buyback is composition change not QE; timing after 5.34% long bond; debt maturity management
buybacks as stabiliser; who controls long end; Treasury plumbing and primary dealers
dealer capital constraints (SLR), hedge funds as marginal Treasury holders, basis trade
basis trade leverage via repo; repo shocks spill to bonds; HFT liquidity can vanish
March 2020 Treasuries not safe; trust cycle; agenda for research segment
Arthur Sepp LGT paper: three trend-following styles
style differences and how many trend managers to hold; blending styles
podification of trend following; netting of fees; teaser on short-term trend research
tick size and short-term trend following; plumbing matters; Niederhoffer introduction
Niederhoffer research legacy: overreaction, clustering, insider trades, empiricism
outro and legal disclaimer, nothing actionable

completeness_estimate: 0.82 - the first reader captured the main Treasury-plumbing chain, index numbers and the trend-style taxonomy; it missed supporting analogies (cocoa, 2000-02 buyback, 1980s dealer failures), the dealer-spread mechanism, CTD switching, Niels's caveats on style labels and costs, and the Niederhoffer ecosystem/Taleb framing.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: someone loses 67% in a single month. Well, we find out once again that uh you know uh leverage hurts or leverage kills.
claims.claim: A fund losing 67% in one month is a reminder that leverage can wipe out capital; such episodes are 'rumblings' of fragile markets.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we're seeing some of those new issues sort of uh have big reversals and usually it's a sign of an overvalued market when there's more stock issuance
claims.claim: Rising equity issuance with new issues reversing is a sign of an overvalued market (late-stage bubble), and a Korean stock bubble just collapsed after a huge run-up.
claims.indicator: equity issuance volume; new issue performance
claims.testable: yes - issuance vs forward returns is testable

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: Intervention usually doesn't work in the foreign exchange markets, but that hasn't stopped the governments to say like we've got to arrest the uh what is going on in the yen market
claims.claim: Joint Japan MoF and Fed yen intervention signals authorities dislike the market direction, but FX intervention usually fails to reverse trends.
claims.direction: yen trend likely persists after intervention

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: But 15 out of 40 is a big deal
claims.claim: A large multi-strategy/market-maker firm reportedly lost $15bn on a single concentrated bet after earning $40bn, suggesting hidden concentration despite many teams and good risk management.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you were a trend follower having uh trading individual stocks potentially it could have been um you know in a downtrend and suddenly it goes up by 177%. What does that tell you um from a riskmanagement perspective?
claims.claim: Trend followers or shorts in single stocks face gap risk of order 177% in a day (Moderna), much more than normal futures, so stock trading needs explicit tail-risk limits.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: there's no question that the individual stock volatility can be much uh greater than what you sort of see in in most futures markets.
claims.claim: Single stocks are generally more volatile than futures markets, though some futures (grains, indices) can still move 20-30% in a month.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the market makers that we have that have been very profitable you know are very different than the market makers of old because they might be taking speculative positions.
claims.claim: Modern market makers take speculative, correlation-based hedge bets across hundreds of stocks, so if historical correlations break they can suffer large losses.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: When inventory goes very low, uh then there's a a decrease in what we call the buffer stock.
claims.claim: Low commodity inventories remove the buffer stock, so users pay almost any price and extreme moves and backwardation follow.
claims.indicator: warehouse inventory levels; futures curve backwardation

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: Looking at inventory levels is critical to understand whether there's going to be a change from contango or to backradation or if there's more whippiness in the front end of a lot of these commodity curves.
claims.claim: Inventory levels help anticipate curve shape changes (contango to backwardation) and front-end volatility, information not contained in the price trend alone.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: copper squeeze draws biggest weekly flow to LME shed since 2020.
claims.claim: A copper spot-to-3-month spread squeeze with the biggest weekly LME inflow since 2020 indicated tight physical supply.
claims.testable: partly - LME stock and spread data

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the demand for oil by China was significantly reduced. So basically they started to pull from their inventory reserves
claims.claim: China cut purchases and drew on reserves to smooth oil price spikes, but as buffers (China and US reserves) deplete a blowoff in oil and refined products becomes the risk.
claims.indicator: Chinese and US strategic oil inventories
claims.testable: partly - reserve data is partially visible

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer has cooled off a little bit in recent days. We're down to kind of a neutral level of 43.
claims.claim: A trend barometer of 43 means a neutral breadth of trending markets in the tracked portfolio.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: VIX index is relatively low. So, so for all of the things we're talking about or all these rumblings, volatility has been relatively low.
claims.claim: Despite stress signals, VIX was low in Aug 2026 and uncertainty had receded from its Ukraine war high.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: This is that let's look at the yen carry trade, you know, which being unwind.
claims.claim: Complexity and ambiguity (unwinding yen carry trade with intervention, unclear Fed policy and Treasury financing) force participants to adjust expectations slowly, creating trends in the fall.
claims.direction: trend opportunities in FX and rates

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Btop 50 up 1.78% for the month of August. Uh up 9.87 for the year.
claims.claim: As of 18 Aug 2026 trend indices were up roughly 9.7-9.9% YTD (BTOP50 9.87%, SG Trend 9.73%, SG CTA 9.7%), short-term traders 4.6%, vs MSCI World 12.3%, S&P total return 12.6%, US Aggregate 0.39%.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG Trend Index, SG Short-Term Traders Index, S&P 500 TR

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: he has said that he's the uh number one salesman for US bonds around the world.
claims.claim: The US Treasury Secretary's role is to ensure buyers for Treasuries as weekly refunding auctions approach $800bn.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we have a lot of these different we'll call it orphan bonds that are away from the benchmark on ther run issue.
claims.claim: Many off-the-run bonds with different coupons are less liquid than on-the-run issues, so there is a yield and price gap between them.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the Treasury Secretary is basically signaling to the market that we have a liquidity problem with an off therun issues.
claims.claim: The Treasury buyback programme (raised from about $2bn to about $4bn a month) swaps off-the-run for new on-the-run issuance, changing composition not total debt, which signals insufficient dealer market-making capacity.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the Treasury long bond hits 5.34% which is like the highest we've seen in god knows how long
claims.claim: Buyback announced right after the long bond hit 5.34% looks like soft yield curve control for the long end.
claims.direction: lower long-end yields from official action

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if the government tells you not to worry that's the time to start
claims.claim: Official reassurance should itself be treated as a warning sign of an underlying problem.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: during the Yellen period there was a tremendous amount of focus on issuing more Treasury bills as opposed to bonds.
claims.claim: Shifting issuance toward bills shortens average maturity and holds down long yields without Fed action; a buyback could be a precursor to bills replacing bonds to relieve the long end.
claims.indicator: Treasury issuance mix (bills vs bonds); average maturity

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the Treasury could step in and be able to buy those cheap bonds that they think is cheap in an effort as part of this buyback program. So, they're actually act acting as uh bond market stabilizers
claims.claim: Treasury buybacks can act as a small bond market stabiliser by buying off-the-run bonds that trade cheap to the curve.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we as trend followers we we don't mind if we have a long-term trend in the short end uh where we can see the path of of um of of interest rates going higher or lower
claims.claim: Trends in short rates follow monetary policy paths and suit trend followers, while the long end can have massive moves if rates truly change.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: there is no exchange for treasuries. Now we do have the futures exchange for futures but the rest of the cash market is over the counters driven by a set of primary government security dealers.
claims.claim: Cash Treasuries trade OTC through primary dealers who also serve as auction conduits.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: because of regulations from the Fed so such as the uh supplemental liquidity ratios is is that there may not be enough capital at primary government security dealers for them to do their job to make markets.
claims.claim: Regulation like the supplementary leverage ratio limits dealer balance sheets so capital for market making is out of proportion to Treasury volume, reducing liquidity.
claims.indicator: dealer balance sheet capacity vs Treasury volume
claims.direction: wider bid-ask when liquidity is scarce

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: hedge funds are the people who are hold some of the biggest holders they may uh be larger than mutual funds in terms of their holdings of treasuries. We're looking at 9% plus of the total
claims.claim: Hedge funds hold over 9% of marketable Treasuries, so the marginal long-end buyer is now levered rather than real money.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the number one trade is the basis trade. So, so the basis trade between the futures and and and cash
claims.claim: The Fed finds the basis trade (cash vs futures, anchored on the cheapest to deliver) is the top hedge fund Treasury trade, and it keeps futures aligned with cash.
claims.indicator: Treasury cash-futures basis; cheapest to deliver

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you've got to use a tremendous amount of leverage on what you think is a fairly low risk low return trade
claims.claim: The Treasury basis trade earns only a few ticks so it is run with extreme repo leverage; any repo market stress would spill into the bond market.
claims.conditions: Fed balance-sheet cuts or short-rate rises

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it certainly reminds me about the the Swiss Frank euro um trade that lots of people loved and felt certain about until the day where the Swiss Frank was let free
claims.claim: Crowded low-risk levered trades can fail suddenly (SNB removing the franc floor).

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the HFT, the high frequency traders like the Citadel and other places that are active in the Treasury market. So, but they're all electronic trading. They're not reporting to the Fed. They don't have specific market making responsibilities.
claims.claim: High-frequency liquidity providers in Treasuries have no obligation to make markets and can switch off in stress, withdrawing liquidity.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: when you look at March of 2020, there was a shortage of liquidity in the market. So we expected that treasuries would act as a safe asset and it didn't act like the safe asset.
claims.claim: In March 2020 Treasuries failed as a safe asset because liquidity vanished, so safety includes the ability to sell at a fair price.
claims.direction: avoid Treasuries as hedge in liquidity crises

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: once you lose the trust of the market uh then uh all hell breaks loose.
claims.claim: Loss of trust in institutions is a slow cycle that, once trust breaks in a market, produces disorderly moves; worth monitoring.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: he defines European is those people who look for s you know high signal to noise trades and look at constant adjustments in their positioning.
claims.claim: The LGT paper (Arthur Sepp) classifies trend followers as European (high signal to noise, dynamic position adjustment), American (breakout with digital positions held until exit) and academic time-series momentum (scaled by return).

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: they actually are fairly similar in terms of their sharp ratios, their draw downs. There might be differences between each one of these. They all do very well during periods when there's a lot of trends.
claims.claim: The three trend styles have similar Sharpe ratios and drawdowns and all do well in strongly trending periods, with nuance in timing.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: probably a good idea to start by looking at people with structural difference now this could one structural difference, right? Could also be the number of markets they trade.
claims.claim: When building a portfolio of managers, diversify by structural differences (markets traded, speed) rather than by style labels, because the future path is unknown.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the number of trend followers you need to be able to replicate a benchmark or replicate is probably less than for some other hedge fund styles.
claims.claim: Fewer trend followers are needed to replicate the trend benchmark than managers in other hedge fund styles.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: I run different trend following models almost as if they're different pods and then what I could do is I can blend those together
claims.claim: Run American, European and time-series momentum models as internal pods, aggregate signals before execution to cut transaction costs while tracking each pod's performance.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there is one other big advantage compared to going out finding three or four or five different managers and that is you get netting of the performance fee.
claims.claim: Blending styles in one fund nets performance fees across models, unlike paying separate fees to several managers.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: short-term trend following just doesn't really work that well.
claims.claim: Research finds short-term trend following has weakened in practice.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if you look at contract futures contracts that have large tick size, you can still make money from short-term trend following. those that have very tight or small tick size, it is very hard to make profits in those markets
claims.claim: Short-term trend profits remain in futures with large (vol-adjusted) tick size, but are competed away by HFT market makers where tick sizes are small.
claims.direction: short-term trend only in large-tick contracts
claims.conditions: small tick size markets dominated by HFT

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: It's more like a vault breakout and then they get out at at you know with completely different uh rules not from a reversal of price
claims.claim: Short-term 'trend following' is typically volatility breakout with different exit rules, not true trend following, so results are not comparable with longer-term trend.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: understanding the plumbing of how markets operate and and and plumbing does matter. So those, you know, tick size matters, you know, who are the players in the market in treasuries matters, how who's getting financing
claims.claim: Market microstructure (tick size, player mix, financing) affects strategy returns as much as model details like breakout length.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: did some extreme uh good research in short-term mean reversion
claims.claim: Niederhoffer research: headline overreaction, round-number price clustering, short-term mean reversion after large moves, and executive insider trades as signals.
claims.direction: fade large moves short term; follow insider buying

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if you cannot count it, you do not know it.
claims.claim: Empiricism: verify with numbers and rigorous backtests; quality of results depends on quality of testing.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: blowups after the uh you know in uh you know in the you know late 90s
claims.claim: Niederhoffer blew up in the late 1990s (and again later) despite empirical rigour, showing tail and leverage risk; he recovered by improving the process.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think now more recently we've had um single stock equities come out as futures. So there might be even more people from our industry attracted to that area.
claims.claim: The new listing of single-stock futures may draw more systematic futures managers into single-name trading, which exposes them to gap risk far beyond that of traditional futures markets.
claims.conditions: relevant for trend followers adding single stocks to a futures universe
claims.testable: partly - jump-risk statistics of single-stock futures versus index futures

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: It could be excessive speculation which is good for the person who is the buyer but you say that what happens when the markets start to normalize you're
claims.claim: Huge single-stock run-ups in AI names (Micron from under 400 in April to about 1,200) look like excessive speculation; when markets normalize the reversal will hurt late buyers, so such moves are a 'rumbling' of fragility.
claims.direction: reversal risk in speculative AI stocks
claims.testable: partly - after-the-fact reversals of extreme multi-month run-ups

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: We saw that in the cocoa market a couple years ago is is that there's just not enough inventory.
claims.claim: Cocoa two years earlier is the analogy for buffer-stock exhaustion: when inventories are too low users bid any price, and the same dynamic is a risk for oil (after Iran-war moves) and metals such as copper.
claims.direction: extreme price spikes and backwardation when inventory is scarce
claims.conditions: only when production needs continuing physical supply and warehouses are depleted
claims.testable: yes - inventory-to-consumption ratios versus subsequent price spikes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: what what the missing and his in his view I think like a billion barrels of oil physical oil what that might lead to
claims.claim: Commodity analyst Adam Rosenswag argues that roughly a billion barrels of physical oil are unaccounted for, which could eventually produce much higher oil prices, though the timing is uncertain.
claims.testable: partly - depends on inventory accounting that is not public in full

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: the first buyback program was in 2000 2002 and at that particular time if you could believe it is that the US government was running a uh uh a you know surplus
claims.claim: Treasury buybacks have precedent: the first programme (2000-2002) was designed when budget surpluses raised fears of running short of long bonds, was stopped when rates were stable and restarted later, so the current expansion reflects liquidity needs rather than a surplus.
claims.testable: partly - small number of historical buyback episodes

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: you're going to either have to increase your bid spread because it's going to be harder to find that buyer and you're going to have to hold that on your balance sheet longer
claims.claim: When Treasuries become less liquid, balance-sheet-constrained dealers must widen bid-ask spreads and hold inventory longer, which they must finance with scarce capital, so liquidity deteriorates exactly when selling pressure rises.
claims.direction: wider spreads and weaker liquidity in stress
claims.conditions: when dealer capital is limited by leverage regulation
claims.testable: yes - dealer inventory and quoted spreads in stress episodes

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: So that that then that means is that there's more opportunities for basis trading profits but also for risk.
claims.claim: More outstanding Treasury issues raise the chance that the cheapest-to-deliver bond switches, which creates both more basis-trade profit opportunities and more risk for the levered funds running them.
claims.conditions: when many different coupons and maturities are outstanding
claims.testable: yes - CTD switch frequency versus basis volatility

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if let's say that the Fed wants to sort of cut its balance sheet okay then that's going to have an impact on on repo financing
claims.claim: Because Treasury positions are financed in repo, a Fed balance-sheet reduction or a rise in short rates tightens repo financing and reverberates from the overnight market through the whole bond market, as with the highly financed secondary Treasury dealers that failed in the 1980s.
claims.direction: funding stress transmits from short end to long end
claims.conditions: when dealers and hedge funds are heavily leveraged through repo
claims.testable: yes - repo spikes versus Treasury market dislocations

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's a lot of of firms based in the US today that uh uses dynamic position sizing
claims.claim: The European/American trend-follower labels are historical rather than geographic: the digital-position 'American' style reflects the era before dynamic sizing tools existed, and today many US firms use dynamic sizing and hybrid breakout-plus-dynamic approaches, so due diligence must examine actual sizing and signal rules, not the label.
claims.testable: yes - classify managers by return-based sizing behaviour

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: where managers start to blend different types of trend following uh as long as it's quote unquote pure trend so you're not deviating from that
claims.claim: Trend managers tend to stay with the style they started with, but programmes that evolve to blend several methodologies (provided each model is good and remains pure trend) can be stronger than a single style, which is a form of diversification inside one programme.
claims.conditions: each component must be a well-built, truly trend-following model

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: transaction cost generally at least in my view is not the biggest hurdle we face uh in in the in the long-term trend following uh trading on exchange futures uh only because transaction cost are low
claims.claim: For long-term trend following in exchange-traded futures, transaction costs are low and not the main hurdle, so the cost saving from netting pod signals before execution is modest and the fee-netting benefit matters more.
claims.conditions: holds for long-horizon trend in liquid futures, not for short-term trend
claims.testable: yes - estimate turnover and cost drag by lookback

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: he viewed it more as an you know evolutionary biology sense an ecosystem that uh so it's not so much markets are efficient but you have to look at what the ecosystem of markets and how they behave
claims.claim: Niederhoffer treated markets as an evolving ecosystem of participants rather than as an efficient pricing machine, so understanding who the players are and how they behave (what is now called market plumbing) is a source of edge.
claims.testable: no - a framework rather than a specific rule

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: if Victor Netherhoffer was the uh true empiricist say Nin Talab was the skeptic and so uh so so you had the quant who said like let's just look at the data and follow the numbers
claims.claim: The Niederhoffer versus Taleb contrast frames a core research dilemma: the empiricist trusts data and rigorous backtests while the skeptic argues that history and statistical data can mislead, and Niederhoffer's blowups show the cost of over-trusting the numbers while his comebacks show the value of improving process.
